{{short description|American mathematician}}
'''Maury Daniel Bramson''' (born 1951 in New York City) is an American mathematician, specializing in probability theory and mathematical statistics.

==Education and career==
Bramson grew up in the Los Angeles area and graduated with a bachelor's degree in mathematics from the [[University of California, Berkeley]] after having also attended the [[University of California, San Diego]] and having participated in the University of California's Education Abroad Program at the [[University of Göttingen]]. He graduated with a master's degree in statistics from [[Stanford University]].<ref name=NAS>{{cite web|title=Maury D. Bramson|website=Member Directory, National Academy of Sciences|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/maury-d-bramson-91psq2/}}</ref> In 1977 he received his PhD from [[Cornell University]] with thesis ''Maximal Displacement of Branching Brownian Motion'' under the supervision of [[Harry Kesten]].<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=22561|title=Maury Daniel Bramson}}</ref> Bramson was an instructor at the [[Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences]]. He was a member of the mathematical faculties of the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]] and the [[University of California, Davis]] before becoming a professor at the [[University of Minnesota]].<ref name=NAS/> He was at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] for the academic year 1995–1996.<ref>{{cite web|title=Maury Bramson|website=Institute for Advanced Study|date=9 December 2019 |url=https://www.ias.edu/scholars/maury-bramson}}</ref>

Bramson's research deals with models of [[interacting particle system]]s, [[stochastic network]]s, and [[branching process]]es. The models are motivated by physical and biological science, engineering, and computer science.<ref name=NAS/>

Bramson was an Invited Speaker at the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] in Berlin in 1998.<ref>{{cite book|author=Bramson, Maury|chapter=State space collapse for queueing networks|title=''In:'' Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians, 1998, Berlin|year=1998|volume=3|pages=213–222|chapter-url=https://www.elibm.org/ft/10011579000}}</ref> He was elected a Fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]] in the class of 2015 for "contributions to stochastic processes and their applications."<ref>{{cite journal|title=2015 Class of the Fellows of the AMS|date=March 2015|journal=Notices of the AMS|volume=62|issue=3|pages=285–287|url=https://www.ams.org/profession/ams-fellows/rnoti-p285.pdf}}</ref> He was elected a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 2017. He is also a Fellow of the [[Institute of Mathematical Statistics]].<ref name=NAS/>
